text: About 3,500 years ago, the Mumun people lived in the south and middle of Korea, many of them in river valleys.
Their name comes from the Korean word for their plain pottery, which had no decoration.
src: an era of Korean prehistory dated to about 1500–300 BCE / Southern and central Korea / many of them in the valleys of tributaries of the Geum River in west-central Korea
It is named after the Korean word for the undecorated, plain cooking and storage vessels

text: They were farmers who grew millet, rice, barley and wheat, and they still hunted and fished too.
They lived in pit-houses, homes built partly below the ground, and some had up to six fireplaces.
src: people also grew millets, barley, wheat and legumes, and went on hunting, fishing and foraging / Rice appeared in the Early Mumun beside the older millet farming
rectangular, semi-subterranean pit-houses / Early Mumun pit-houses could have as many as six hearths

text: Later, some important people were buried in large stone tombs with bronze daggers and jade.
Bronze was rare, though, and most of their tools were still made of stone.
src: megalithic burials with deep shaft interments and substantial pavements of rounded cobblestones held bronze daggers, jade and red-burnished pottery / Some were especially large
Early bronze objects are rare / Stone remained the main material for tools

text: Their way of life reached as far as Jeju Island and western Japan.
src: its farthest reach appears to have been Jeju Island and western Japan

text: About 2,300 years ago iron arrived, and the Mumun time came to an end.
But the Mumun began a long tradition of rice farming in Korea that lasts to this day.
src: it ended around 300 BCE as iron arrived
It began a long tradition of rice farming in Korea that links it with the present day
